items.q: Two libraries in your graph need different versions of the same artifact. What does Gradle do? How do you make it pick yours?
shortAnswer: Gradle resolves the graph in one pass and picks the highest version satisfying every constraint. A direct declaration in your module beats a transitive one.
When no version satisfies everyone, resolution fails with an error that lists the paths, so you can see exactly who asked for what.
To fix it, add the version you want explicitly, tighten with a `constraints` block or `strictly`, and confirm the winner with `dependencyInsight`.
items.answer:
#### What Gradle actually does
Gradle resolves the entire graph at once and, by default, picks the **highest version** of every artifact that satisfies the constraints it sees. Conflict resolution is winner-takes-all across configurations, so two modules asking for `gson:2.10` and `gson:2.11` resolve to 2.11. When no single version satisfies everyone, resolution fails with an error that lists each requesting path — read the paths, not just the versions.

#### Why your catalog doesn't fix it
A version catalog is just a variable; declaring `okhttp = "4.12.0"` in your own module is a *direct* dependency, and direct wins over transitive. That is the first fix: add the version you want explicitly. If that is not enough, a `constraints { }` block tightens the floor for the whole graph, and `strictly` forbids everything outside a range — useful when a transitive wants a version you know is broken.

#### Finding and pinning
`./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --configuration debugRuntimeClasspath --dependency gson` shows who requested what and which version won. `force()` still exists, but it is a blunt project-wide hammer that hides the real conflict from future authors — prefer explicit declarations and constraints that read clearly in review.

code.caption: Direct wins, constraints tighten, force is the last resort

followUps: How does `strictly` differ from an ordinary version declaration?
What does dependency locking change about how versions are chosen?
Where would you look in a build scan to find who pulled in a conflicting version?
traps: Claiming the version catalog decides — it is a variable; resolution is graph-wide highest-version.
Reaching for `force()` first — it masks the conflict instead of resolving it and surprises consumers.

items.q: How do you share build logic across many modules? Why is buildSrc the wrong home once it grows?
shortAnswer: A convention plugin centralizes shared configuration — the Android DSL, Kotlin options, testing, lint — and modules apply it with `plugins { id("...") }`.
buildSrc works but recompiles as one unit and is uncacheable: any edit invalidates configuration and build caches, costing seconds, and can't be shared or versioned.
The scalable home is an included build, `includeBuild("build-logic")`. Its plugins are versioned, compiled and cached independently, and reusable across repos.
items.answer:
#### The plugin, not the script
The convention-plugin pattern is a Gradle plugin that centralizes shared configuration — the Android DSL, Kotlin compiler options, testing setup, lint, Dagger. Modules apply it with `plugins { id("...") }`, so a new module inherits the whole house style in two lines, and a change is reviewed once instead of across fifty build scripts.

#### Why buildSrc scales badly
buildSrc is compiled automatically and is a *hard dependency of every build*. Any edit recompiles it, and because its outputs are not cacheable, that recompile cascades into the configuration cache and the build cache — every developer and CI run pays seconds per invocation even for an unrelated change. It also cannot be versioned or shared between separate builds, so a two-repo company duplicates it and drifts.

#### The included build
The scalable home is a separate `build-logic` project registered with `includeBuild("build-logic")` in the root settings file. Each plugin is published internally through the `gradlePlugin { }` DSL inside that build, resolved like any dependency, compiled and cached independently, and reusable across repos. Gradle's own guidance moved here explicitly: buildSrc is fine for small projects, but once the plugin set grows, an included build is the way.

code.caption: An included build with one convention plugin

followUps: What does the configuration cache do to buildSrc that it cannot do to an included build?
How do you version a convention plugin so one repo can depend on another's?
When is buildSrc still the right call?
traps: Calling buildSrc 'fine as projects grow' without naming the invalidation mechanism — the interviewer is probing why it stops scaling.
Describing convention plugins without the mechanism: they are real plugins published and resolved, not script import.

items.q: A multi-module Android build is slow. How do you find the slowest part? What structural choices fix it?
shortAnswer: Start with a build scan — `./gradlew assembleDebug --scan`: it splits configuration vs execution time, task durations, cache hit rates, and the critical path.
Most multi-module slowness is unnecessary recompilation: `api` leaks types onto every consumer, so editing one module recompiles everything downstream; `implementation` limits it.
Keep modules coarse enough to earn their overhead, apply only the plugins each needs, enable parallel, caching, and the config cache — then re-run the scan.
items.answer:
#### Measure first
Before touching structure, run `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --scan`. A build scan breaks time into configuration versus execution, lists every task with its duration, shows cache hit and from-cache rates, and traces the **critical path** — the chain of tasks the build cannot shorten. `--profile` writes the same breakdown to `build/reports/profile`. If configuration dominates, the fix is convention plugins and the configuration cache; if execution dominates, it is task reruns.

#### Why tasks rerun
The dominant cost in multi-module builds is unnecessary recompilation. A module's Kotlin compile reruns whenever any input changes — and an `api` dependency leaks its types onto consumers, so editing a shared module recompiles everything downstream. `implementation` confines the blast radius to one module. The same logic applies to tests: a module's test task should not sit on the critical path of `assembleDebug`.

#### Structural levers
Keep modules coarse enough to earn their overhead, apply only the plugins each needs — a plain Kotlin module should not apply AGP — and enable `org.gradle.parallel`, `org.gradle.caching`, and the configuration cache. Then re-run the identical scan and confirm the critical path actually moved. The scan is the before-and-after instrument; without it you are optimizing assumptions.

code.caption: Measure, then read the report
code.src:
# Measure configuration vs execution and the critical path
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --scan --profile

# Profile report: build/reports/profile/profile-2026-08-13-*.html
# Scan: browser report with per-task duration, cache hit rates, critical path

# Why did a task rerun? Inspect its inputs
./gradlew :feature:checkout:compileDebugKotlin --info

followUps: What shows up in a scan when a module recompiles for no reason?
When does adding a module make a build slower rather than faster?
How would you apply the configuration cache to a build that mutates state during execution?
traps: Optimizing before measuring — the whole point of the scan is to remove guesswork.
Prescribing `api` everywhere for convenience; the interview is probing whether you know it widens recompilation.

items.q: Why is kapt a build-time tax? How do you move a module to KSP2?
shortAnswer: kapt lets Java annotation processors run on Kotlin code: it compiles Kotlin, generates Java stubs, then runs javac over them — 2-3× KSP's wall time.
KSP2 reads Kotlin symbols from the compiler frontend — no stubs, faster, multiplatform. Migration: swap `kapt("...")` for `ksp("...")`, drop `kotlin-kapt`.
The blocker is third-party processors with no KSP provider. Those keep you on kapt, isolated to the module that actually needs them.
items.answer:
#### The tax
kapt exists to run *Java* annotation processors on Kotlin code. It compiles your Kotlin, generates a Java stub for every file, then runs javac over the stubs — a full second compilation. That double compilation is the tax: typically two to three times KSP's wall time, and single-platform, so it blocks Kotlin Multiplatform modules entirely. Stub generation also degrades on Kotlin-only constructs such as companion-object constants, which is why some processors see missing values.

#### KSP2
KSP2 reads Kotlin symbols directly from the compiler frontend — no stubs, faster, multiplatform — and it became the default for new projects on the Kotlin 2.x line. Room, Hilt, Moshi, Glide and most Google libraries already ship KSP processors. Migration is mechanical: apply the KSP Gradle plugin, swap every `kapt("...")` for `ksp("...")`, and delete the `kotlin-kapt` plugin from the module.

#### What still blocks you
The holdout is the long tail of third-party processors with no KSP provider. You cannot force them from your side; the pragmatic move is to keep kapt only in the module that needs that one processor — kapt and KSP coexist fine across modules — file an issue upstream, and retire kapt there once a provider ships.

code.caption: The mechanical swap: kapt -> KSP2

followUps: Which Kotlin constructs does stub generation make kapt process incorrectly?
Why is kapt incompatible with a Kotlin Multiplatform module?
How do you migrate a project where one processor still lacks KSP support?
traps: Describing kapt as 'slow' without the mechanism — it is the stub-generation-plus-javac double compile that is the tax.
Claiming every library supports KSP today; the honest answer includes the holdouts and the module-scoped workaround.

refs.title: Kotlin docs — Java annotation processing to KSP reference

items.q: What are product flavors and build types, and how do a variant's source sets and dependencies come together?
shortAnswer: A build type describes how a build is packaged — debug is debuggable, release shrinks and signs. Flavors describe what it contains: free vs paid.
AGP crosses every flavor with every build type, producing variants like `freeDebug` and `paidRelease`, each with a merged source set, manifest, and APK.
Dependencies use the same naming — `debugImplementation`, `freeImplementation`, `freeDebugImplementation` — so LeakCanary or an ads SDK ships only to the variants that want it.
items.answer:
#### The matrix
A build type describes *how* a build is packaged: `debug` is debuggable with no shrinking; `release` shrinks, obfuscates, and signs. Product flavors describe *what* it contains: `free` versus `paid`, or a `dev` API endpoint versus `prod`. AGP crosses every flavor with every build type, producing `freeDebug`, `freeRelease`, `paidDebug`, `paidRelease` — each a full variant with its own APK and merged resources. Add one dimension per axis with `flavorDimensions`, and every combination is built, so keep dimensions few: each one multiplies build time.

#### Source sets
Every variant merges source sets in a fixed order: `main`, then the flavor, then the build type, then the full variant. `app/src/paidDebug/` overrides `app/src/paid/` overrides `app/src/main/`. That gives four granularity levels for code and resources — a paid-only Billing screen lives in the paid source set, not behind a runtime `if`.

#### Variant-aware dependencies
The same naming extends to dependencies: `freeImplementation(...)`, `debugImplementation(...)`, `freeDebugImplementation(...)`, plus `androidTestImplementation` for tests. A crash reporter ships to every variant, LeakCanary only to `debugImplementation`, billing only to `paid`. The manifest can differ per variant too — permissions included only for the flavors that need them.

code.caption: Flavors, build types, and variant-aware dependencies

followUps: What happens to variant names when you add a second flavor dimension?
How do you share code between flavors that is not identical but is close?
When does a product flavor stop being the right tool and a separate app module start?
traps: Confusing build types with flavors — one is packaging, the other is content.
Forgetting the source-set precedence order, which is the whole mechanism behind per-variant code.

items.q: How do you sign a release build, and what does Play App Signing change about key management?
shortAnswer: An APK's signature lets the OS and the store verify an update comes from the same developer. A mismatched key fails install or upload.
The signing config lives in `build.gradle.kts`; the keystore and passwords never go in VCS — inject from env vars or a gitignored `gradle.properties`.
Play App Signing separates your upload key from the app signing key Google holds. That's what makes key recovery and rotation possible at all.
items.answer:
#### Why signing exists
A signature is how Android and the store trust that an update comes from the same developer. A mismatched key produces `INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE` on the device and a rejected upload in the Play Console. The signing config is declared in `build.gradle.kts` — store file, alias, passwords — but the keystore and its secrets must never be committed: inject them from environment variables or a gitignored `gradle.properties`, and never lose the only copy of a key you cannot recover.

#### Play App Signing
With Play App Signing you upload an **upload key** and Google re-signs with the app signing key it holds in custody. The real key never leaves Google's infrastructure, which buys two things: you can *recover* a lost upload key by signing a proof APK and requesting a reset in the console, and the app signing key can be **rotated** without breaking existing installs. Rotation propagates over a few days; Play pauses uploads during the window, and devices already running updates signed with the old key stay installed.

#### Rotation mechanics
The console exports the new key, you re-sign a test APK, and Play verifies it before propagation. Because the store blocks new uploads until propagation completes, rotate deliberately — in a low-release window, not mid-campaign. Android 9+ also supports in-app rotation via APK Signature Scheme v3, but for store apps Play App Signing is the normal route.

code.caption: Signing config reading secrets from the environment

followUps: What happens if you lose the upload key with and without Play App Signing?
Why does Play block uploads during key rotation?
How do APK Signature Scheme v3 and v4 differ, and which devices support what?
traps: Treating the keystore as an artifact you can commit — the first question is how secrets get in and stay out of VCS.
Not knowing Play App Signing is what makes key recovery and rotation possible at all.

items.q: You add a library; the release crashes after shrinking. How do R8 rules work? What are consumer rules?
shortAnswer: R8 shrinks, optimizes, and obfuscates. Shrinking deletes classes and members no live code references, including anything reached only by reflection, Gson, or JNI.
Rules are patterns: `-keep` pins a class or member, `-keepclassmembers` keeps selected members of matching classes, `-keepattributes` preserves metadata.
A library ships `consumerProguardFiles` in the AAR, merged into every consuming app's R8 run automatically — the library declares its reflective surface.
items.answer:
#### What R8 actually removes
R8 has three jobs: **shrink** (delete unreachable classes and members), **optimize** (rewrite code), and **obfuscate** (rename). The classic failure is a release-only crash: code reached only by reflection, `Class.forName`, Gson or serialization, or JNI looks unreachable to R8, which proves it unused and deletes it. Debug builds run with shrinking off, so the code is there — the crash is the shrinker, not the library.

#### The rules
A `-keep` pins a class or member so it survives: `-keep class com.example.ApiClient { *; }`. `-keepclassmembers` keeps selected members of any matching class — the classic `@SerializedName` fields — and `-keepattributes` preserves metadata the runtime needs, like `Signature`, `Annotation`, `InnerClasses`, and `EnclosingMethod`. Rules are patterns, so write the narrowest rule that protects the reflective surface; `-dontwarn` suppresses missing-class warnings but should not be a reflex.

#### Consumer rules
When your library builds, its `consumerProguardFiles` are packaged into the AAR and **merged into every consuming app's R8 run automatically**. App authors cannot know your reflective surface, so declaring it in the library is the contract: keep what your library needs reflectively, and consumers shrink safely. Skip it, and every consumer discovers your crashes for you.

code.caption: App shrink config and a library's consumer rules
consumer-rules.pro — the library's reflective surface

followUps: Why does a release crash when debug never does, even with the same code paths?
What happens if two libraries' consumer rules conflict?
How does `-keep` differ from `-keepnames`?
traps: Blaming the library instead of the shrinker — the interview is about R8 deleting reflective surface.
Answering with `-dontwarn` as the general fix rather than precise `-keep` rules and `-keepattributes`.

items.q: How do you publish an Android library module to a Maven repository? What ships in the artifact?
shortAnswer: You publish an AAR, not source. `maven-publish` registers a publication from the release component; the POM carries your dependencies so consumers resolve them transitively.
Maven Central adds GPG signing, a sources jar, and a staging flow through Sonatype before anything is released.
The modern shape is `singleVariant("release") { withSourcesJar() }`, and the artifact ships consumer ProGuard rules embedded, so shrinking never breaks on the consumer side.
items.answer:
#### What gets published
You publish an **AAR**, not source. The `maven-publish` plugin registers a publication from the module's release component — `from(components["release"])` — which bundles the compiled classes, Android resources, manifest, and any consumer ProGuard rules into one artifact, with a POM carrying your dependencies so consumers resolve them transitively. Publish the release variant, never debug.

#### The flow
Maven Central goes through a staging repository: sign the artifacts with GPG via the `signing` plugin, upload to the Sonatype staging repo, verify the content, then release. Coordinate `groupId`, `artifactId`, and `version` carefully, and publish the sources jar — many consumers and IDEs expect it. The clean declaration is `singleVariant("release") { withSourcesJar() }`, which states exactly what the artifact contains instead of leaking debug and release variants.

#### Making it consumable
Set `isPreserveFileTimestamps = false` and reproducible file order so two publishes of the same version are byte-identical. Never republish an existing version with different content — checksums, caches, and build systems treat the coordinate as immutable forever. Publish from CI from a tagged version with a changelog; a library people cannot reproduce or explain is a library they stop upgrading.

code.caption: Publish one release variant, signed, to Sonatype staging

followUps: Why must a published version never be republished with different content?
What does the POM carry that makes a library usable without extra setup?
How does Maven Central staging differ from publishing to a private repo?
traps: Publishing the debug variant by default — the interview checks whether you know the release component is the artifact.
Forgetting sources and signing, which are what make the artifact consumable on Maven Central specifically.

items.q: What does it take to make an Android build reproducible? How do you guard against a compromised dependency?
shortAnswer: A reproducible build means identical inputs yield byte-identical outputs: Gradle's reproducible-archive flags remove timestamps and entry order, and R8 + AGP output is deterministic.
Gradle's dependency verification pins every resolved artifact to a SHA-256 in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`, checked on every download — tampering fails the build loudly.
The full defense layers verification on locking and repository hygiene: lock dynamic versions, keep to `google()` and `mavenCentral()`, review generated metadata like code.
items.answer:
#### Reproducibility
Reproducible means identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. In Gradle: set `isPreserveFileTimestamps = false` and `isReproducibleFileOrder = true` on archive tasks so timestamps and entry order stop leaking; R8 and AGP output is deterministic, so what remains is build IDs, absolute paths, and times baked into generated code or resources. Then `clean assemble` twice must hash to the same AAB — assert it in CI. Reproducibility is what makes verification meaningful: if the artifact is deterministic, you can prove what shipped.

#### The threat and the tool
The supply-chain risk is a compromised dependency — a hijacked account, a malicious version, a poisoned mirror. Gradle's **dependency verification** (`gradle/verification-metadata.xml`) pins every resolved artifact to a SHA-256 that Gradle checks at download time and fails the build on any mismatch. It is trusted once when generated with `--write-verification-metadata`, then committed and reviewed like source — a new dependency version shows up as a metadata diff.

#### The layered defense
Checksums alone are not enough. **Dependency locking** freezes dynamic versions so `latest.release` cannot silently move; keep the repository allowlist to `google()` and `mavenCentral()`; ban `mavenLocal()` and `flatDir` from shared builds; pin plugin versions in the catalog; and generate a CycloneDX SBOM at release so consumers can audit what you shipped. Each layer is cheap, and together they turn a hijacked dependency into a loud failure instead of a silent supply.

code.caption: Reproducible archives and the committed verification metadata
gradle/verification-metadata.xml (generated, then committed)
code.src:
<verification-metadata>
    <components>
        <component group="com.squareup.okhttp3" name="okhttp" version="4.12.0">
            <artifact name="okhttp-4.12.0.aar">
                <sha256 value="ab120c...f9e7" origin="Generated by Gradle"/>
            </artifact>
        </component>
    </components>
</verification-metadata>

followUps: How do you bootstrap verification metadata without trusting the very network you fear?
What does dependency locking change versus a fixed version in the catalog?
Why is a deterministic build a prerequisite for meaningful supply-chain verification?
traps: Treating reproducibility as just 'same Gradle version' — the mechanism is timestamps, ordering, and baked-in environment.
Reaching for checksums as the whole answer; the layered story (locking, repos, plugins, SBOM) is what a senior answer shows.

items.q: How do you add custom lint rules? How do you adopt lint in CI without drowning in legacy issues?
shortAnswer: Lint is pluggable. A custom `IssueRegistry` with detectors runs in the same report as the built-in checks, wired via `lintChecks(project(":lint-rules"))`.
A baseline snapshots today's issues so lint reports only new ones — adopt lint without a mass-cleanup gate; the baseline shrinks as fixes land.
In CI, gate on lint: fail on errors, promote your team's rules to error severity, regenerate the baseline deliberately — a debt ledger, not a muffler.
items.answer:
#### What lint gives you
Lint is a static-analysis framework: `./gradlew lint` runs hundreds of built-in checks and emits HTML and XML reports. It is also pluggable — a custom `IssueRegistry` with detectors runs in the same report as the built-ins, wired into a module with `lintChecks(project(":lint-rules"))`. Detectors can scan whole files (`SourceCodeScanner`) or visit specific nodes and call `report()` with a precise location. Each rule declares an id, severity, explanation, and category, so it behaves exactly like a built-in: warnings, errors, and quickfixes.

#### Adopting on legacy code
A baseline is the mechanism that makes lint adoptable: `lint { baseline = file("lint-baseline.xml") }` snapshots the existing issues, and lint then reports only *new* ones. CI fails on regressions without requiring a mass-cleanup gate, and the baseline shrinks as teams fix the backlog. Regenerate it deliberately — it is a debt ledger, not a muffler.

#### Gating in CI
Gate on the variant that matters: run `./gradlew :app:lintDebug` with `abortOnError = true`, and promote your team's rules to `Severity.ERROR` so they actually block a PR. Tune severities per module — a check that always fails gets disabled, which is worse than a check that never fires.

code.caption: A custom rule registry and the app wiring

followUps: How does the baseline interact with the --final gate when new rules are added?
When would you disable a built-in check, and what are the risks?
What is the difference between a lint baseline and merely suppressing warnings?
traps: Dumping lint on a legacy codebase with no baseline — CI fails on thousands of pre-existing issues and lint gets disabled.
Treating the baseline as permanent; it must shrink and be regenerated deliberately.
